this candidate generalizes perturbation as a general diagnostic principle.","The source context may involve trained individuals; here the subjects are non-experts, which changes the interpretation of perturbation results."],"overturn_conditions":["If the checklist is shown to be robust to all practically achievable perturbations, the causal vs. correlational distinction may not matter for reliability.","If the expert's intuition is shown to be equally vulnerable to perturbations, the diagnostic does not distinguish panel from expert reliability.","If perturbation testing is shown to be impossible for the class of tasks in question, this candidate's diagnostic is untestable."],"shared_structure":["SRC_007 discusses adversarial perturbations that modify inputs to satisfy checklist items, which is exactly the counterfactual test proposed here for distinguishing causal tracking from compliance.","SRC_001's mechanist stance supports the assumption that reliability must be grounded in causal mechanisms, not just correlations.","Both this candidate and SRC_007 use perturbation as a probe for the validity of checklist-based judgments."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_007","SRC_001"],"transfer_claims":["The perturbation-based diagnostic from SRC_007 transfers directly: if you can perturb an item to satisfy the checklist without changing the outcome, the panel is tracking compliance.","The mechanist assumption from SRC_001 transfers: reliability requires tracking the causal mechanism, not just satisfying a procedural checklist.","The failure mode identified in SRC_007\u2014that perturbations cannot satisfy their own success criterion\u2014transfers as a warning that the diagnostic may be practically limited."]},"claim":"The reliability gain is genuine only if the checklist encodes causal features of the outcome and mere compliance tracks correlates. The diagnostic is perturbation invariance: a genuine checklist's items, when satisfied, should not be bypassable by spurious changes that leave the causal determinants of the outcome untouched. If a perturbation can satisfy the checklist while changing the outcome, the panel is tracking compliance, not reliability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the outcome is determined by a complex interaction of features such that no simple causal feature list exists, the checklist cannot encode causal determinants and the causal vs. correlational distinction is moot.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert's intuition is itself tracking correlates rather than causes, the expert has no advantage over a bad checklist.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the perturbation required to test causal vs. correlational structure is practically impossible or alters the task so much that the checklist is no longer applicable, the diagnostic is unimplementable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Objectively-verifiable outcomes have causal determinants. A well-constructed checklist operationalizes these determinants. A poorly constructed one operationalizes correlates. Non-experts following a good checklist are reliable because they are checking the causal chain. Non-experts following a bad checklist are compliant but unreliable because they are checking a spurious chain. The expert's intuition, if reliable, implicitly tracks the causal structure. The diagnostic is therefore counterfactual: modify an item so that the checklist is still satisfied but the causal determinants of the outcome are altered. If the panel's judgment does not change, it is tracking checklist compliance. If it changes, the checklist is encoding genuine causal signal.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
